# Preface {.unnumbered}

This is a working draft of the textbook for GEOG 215, Introduction to Spatial Data Science, built from the course lectures.

Every chapter is a runnable Quarto document. The R code in each chapter runs when the book is built, so the tables and maps you see come from the code printed beside them.

## About this book

This is an interactive textbook specifically designed and written for this class, GEOG 215. 

## How this book is organized

The chapters are grouped into six units. Each unit opens with a page that summarizes its chapters.

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="textbook"}
Each chapter through Chapter 22 is followed by a chapter quiz you can take as many times as you like. Units 1 to 5 end with a unit quiz that mixes questions from all of the unit's chapter quizzes, for reviewing a whole unit at once.
:::

**[Unit 1: R and Spatial Data Science](units/unit-1.qmd)** (Chapters 1–5) sets up everything else. It explains what spatial data science is and why location matters, then gets you working in R, RStudio, and R Markdown, with R's basic building blocks: vectors, data types, and data frames. It ends with `if` statements, loops, and writing your own functions, so you can make decisions and repeat work in code.

**[Unit 2: Into the Tidyverse](units/unit-2.qmd)** (Chapters 6–9) introduces the tidyverse. Working with a year of flights from New York's airports, you learn the dplyr verbs that filter, sort, select, change, and summarize data, chained together with the pipe, and then turn the results into graphs with ggplot2.

**[Unit 3: Maps and Geographic Data](units/unit-3.qmd)** (Chapters 10–14) moves from graphs to maps. You make thematic maps of the UNC campus with tmap, then step back to see how the real world becomes geographic data: the vector and raster data models, the file formats that store them, and the datums, coordinate systems, and map projections that give every feature its location. It ends by getting geographic data from the places that publish it: the US Census Bureau, through the APIs that let your code download its data directly, and the ArcGIS servers that publish many government GIS layers.

**[Unit 4: Spatial Analysis](units/unit-4.qmd)** (Chapters 15–17) starts to analyze spatial data. You join tables by a shared column and by location, explore variables with descriptive statistics, plots, and maps, and describe where features are with spatial statistics such as the mean center. Along the way you put your own R functions to work.

**[Unit 5: Statistics and Science](units/unit-5.qmd)** (Chapters 18–22) turns data into evidence. You compare groups with p-values and ANOVA, model relationships with linear regression, and put it all together in a reproducible spatial data science project. It ends by asking whether near things are more related than distant things: you measure distance, define neighbors and weight matrices, and test for clustering and hot spots with the Average Nearest Neighbor ratio, Moran's I, and Getis-Ord Gi\*.

**[Unit 6: Next Steps](units/unit-6.qmd)** (Chapters 23–24) looks beyond the course. You turn your maps into interactive dashboards with leaflet, flexdashboard, crosstalk, and Shiny, and then look at where spatial data science is used, the advanced topics that build on this book, such as remote sensing, space-time modeling, and GeoAI, and the UNC courses and careers that come next.
